I understand why you’d arrive at that conclusion—if the text itself says these things, then everything else you’ve heard about politics and culture can feel like an attempt to dodge the central issue. And you’re right that there exist verses in the Qur’an that, if stripped of context, appear to command violence. It would be dishonest for me to pretend otherwise. The question is what those verses actually mean in context and how they’ve been understood by mainstream Islamic tradition.

Let’s look directly at a few of the verses often cited, because that’s the best way to see whether the text itself is the “real source” of violence.

**The sword verse (9:5)** is probably the most quoted: “When the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists wherever you find them, capture them, besiege them, and lie in wait for them at every place of ambush. But if they repent, establish prayer, and give zakah, let them go their way.” If you read only that, it sounds like a blanket order to kill non-Muslims.

Now read the two verses immediately before it (9:1–4), which provide the context: a specific treaty between the Muslims of Medina and a group of polytheist tribes had been repeatedly violated by those tribes, who had attacked the Muslims. The Qur’an explicitly exempts those polytheists who honored their treaties and says to fulfill agreements with them. So the command is directed at a specific set of aggressors during an active conflict, not at all non-Muslims forever. And as you quoted, even those are offered amnesty if they cease hostilities and pledge peace.

Then look at 9:6, directly after: “If any one of the polytheists seeks asylum with you, grant him asylum so that he may hear the word of God, then deliver him to his place of safety.” That’s a clear mandate to protect an enemy combatant who asks for safety and to escort him to a secure place. A text that says “kill them,” immediately followed by “but protect them and escort them to safety if they seek peace,” cannot honestly be read as a standing order to murder all non-Muslims.

**Another example: 9:29**, “Fight those who do not believe in God and the Last Day… until they pay the jizyah tax willingly while subdued.” This verse is often presented as proof that Islam commands perpetual war. But historically, Muslim jurists understood this as a specific regulation for a particular kind of conflict with the Byzantine Empire—the surrounding verses explicitly discuss those who broke treaties and refused peace. Classical exegetes like Al-Tabari and Al-Qurtubi interpret it within that framework, not as a universal command. Moreover, the same Qur’an (2:256) says “There is no compulsion in religion,” which mainstream scholars for centuries understood as banning forced conversion. You can’t forcibly convert someone you’re ordered to fight until they submit; paying a tax under a peace treaty is a political arrangement, not a spiritual one. (And to be clear, modern Muslim thinkers have critiqued the classical jizyah system, but the point is the original context wasn’t “slaughter them all.”)

**How do Muslim scholars reconcile such verses?** They use a standard principle: the Qur’an must be interpreted in its entirety, not as isolated snippets. Verses revealed early in Mecca, when Muslims were a persecuted minority, emphasize patience, non-retaliation, and peaceful persuasion: “Bear patiently what they say, and leave them with dignity” (73:10). Later Medinan verses permit armed struggle only when the community faced existential military threat: “Permission [to fight] is given to those against whom war is being wrongfully waged, and God is indeed able to help them” (22:39). Even those are hedged with strict restraints: “Fight in the way of God those who fight you, but do not transgress limits. God does not love transgressors” (2:190). Classical jurists then developed detailed rules of war based on these verses and the Prophet’s example: don’t kill non-combatants, don’t destroy crops or animals, don’t mutilate bodies, offer terms of peace whenever possible. If someone today rips a verse out of that framework and claims it commands random violence, they’re violating the methodological rules that Muslim jurists themselves set.

**That’s exactly what extremist groups do.** A person like Osama bin Laden had no formal Islamic legal training; he and his ilk ignore context, scholarly consensus, and the vast body of interpretive tradition to weaponize snippets of scripture. Their ideology is literally a modern political innovation—in the Islamic sense, a *bid’ah*, a heretical departure from orthodoxy. They do the same thing violent extremists have done with the Bible, the Torah, or the Bhagavad Gita: they strip away the interpretative framework and use the remaining raw words as a blunt instrument.

Now, does this mean Islam has no challenging texts? Of course it does. The Hebrew Bible has commands to slaughter entire Canaanite cities, and the New Testament has passages that have been used to justify anti-Semitism for centuries. A mature study of any scripture involves confronting difficult material. But “the Qur’an tells people to kill unbelievers” as a blanket statement is simply false; it tells people to fight in self-defense within strict rules, to honor treaties, and to cease the moment the enemy sues for peace. The vast, overwhelming bulk of the text is about mercy, justice, worship, and moral living. Thousands of its verses—like “If a person kills one person, it is as if he has killed all of humanity, and if a person saves one life, it is as if he has saved all of humanity” (5:32)—explicitly teach the opposite of random violence.

The course you’re considering would let you see this for yourself by reading the primary sources alongside scholarly commentary, rather than relying on secondhand lists of “gotcha” verses. They’d say: yes, those things happened, horribly, but they’re not the whole story; they’re a misuse of a tradition that also built hospitals, inspired abolitionists, and taught love of enemy. We don’t judge modern Judaism by that. We understand it as a founding narrative, not a standing order. Why the different standard?

Religion is the vocabulary local people have to express resistance, identity, and grievance. When Chechens fought Russia, they framed it as jihad. When Iraqis fought American occupation, they framed it as jihad. Are those conflicts about the theology of the Qur’an, or about power, land, and survival, expressed in the only ideological language available that carries weight? Some defend the judgment according to tribal law; others question its historicity or morality. That wrestling is itself a sign that the tradition isn’t monolithic in celebrating violence.

**Why the difference? Because Nazism and Islam are not the same kind of thing, and they don’t operate on the same scale or with the same internal diversity.**

Nazism was a specific political ideology that arose in a specific place and time, had a clear hierarchy of texts (*Mein Kampf*, the Party program), a single Führer, and a core doctrine of racial extermination. It’s the governing faith of Indonesia, Senegal, and Turkey just as much as Afghanistan. It is practiced by people who are themselves victims of the very terrorist groups you’re pointing to. To call the entire thing—every believer, every text, every tradition—“evil” based on its worst episodes and worst actors is a category error. But calling an entire religion “evil” is a closing of inquiry, not an opening.** It’s a decision to stop looking at the parts that don’t fit the verdict. The course wouldn’t stop you from reaching a negative conclusion. But it would let you reach it after genuinely examining the full range, rather than using the worst as a shortcut. That’s not special treatment. That’s the difference between a verdict and a real understanding.
